draft.title: Melatonin and the SCN
card: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) is a small area of the hypothalamus. It acts as the body's main clock for the sleep-wake cycle.
The SCN receives information about light from the eyes. Light levels tell it whether it is day or night.
When light falls in the evening, the SCN signals the pineal gland, a small gland in the brain. The pineal gland then releases melatonin, a hormone that makes us sleepy.
Bright light, especially in the morning, reduces melatonin release. This helps keep us alert during the day.
draft.remember: Light reaches the SCN, the SCN directs the pineal gland, and the pineal gland controls melatonin.

a.q: What is the role of the suprachiasmatic nucleus in the sleep-wake cycle?
opts: It uses light information to signal melatonin release
It releases melatonin directly into the bloodstream
It records brain waves while a person sleeps
It detects tiredness from muscle activity
a.why: The SCN receives light information from the eyes and signals the pineal gland. The pineal gland, not the SCN, releases melatonin, which is why the option about direct release is wrong.
a.clue: Which structure sends the signal, and which one releases the hormone?

b.q: Jin works night shifts in Geelong and sleeps in a bright room in the morning. Why might he find it hard to fall asleep?
opts: Bright light reduces melatonin release signalled by the SCN
Bright light makes the pineal gland release more melatonin
Darkness stops the SCN from receiving any signals
Melatonin is released only by the SCN in daylight
b.why: Light reaching the eyes reaches the SCN, which reduces the signal for melatonin release, so Jin feels less sleepy. The option that light increases melatonin has the effect reversed.
b.clue: Think about what light does to melatonin.

a.best: It uses light information to signal melatonin release

b.best: Bright light reduces melatonin release signalled by the SCN
